entries.name: The Church of the East — Three Patriarchates
entries.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2): the sources are mostly outside witnesses. Its window runs from 1650 to 1815, the years between the two entries on either side of it. Not yet reviewed.
entries.sourcing:
The evidence is thin. Most texts come from outside the mountain church.

Badger was an English churchman who disliked Rome's work. Wigram led a church mission to the Assyrians. Labourt wrote for a Catholic reference work.

Malech was an Assyrian Protestant from Urmia. He gives the mountain side in a few lines. Labourt says few documents survive for these years.
entries.relationsSummary: This entry carries the Church of the East from 1650 to 1815. It follows the Schism of 1552 and leads on to the Chaldean Consolidation. Popes and missionaries shaped these years, and the entry on the Catholic Church of the Ancien Régime tells their side.
entries.why: The Church of the East had two patriarchs in 1650, one in the mountains and one on the plain. In 1681 the pope named a third, at Diyarbakır. In 1778 the patriarch of the plain died of plague, and the next day his nephew Hormizd turned to Rome. He wrote down the date: 30 April.
entries.longDescription:
The Church of the East began these years with two rival patriarchs. One lived in the mountains of Hakkari. Malech says a patriarch of that line, Denkha Shimon, later moved its seat to the village of Qudshanis. The other lived on the plain, at Alqosh and Mosul.

Each patriarch of the plain held an order from the Sultan, called a firman. It confirmed his power over his people in the empire. The mountain patriarchs had no such order. Badger writes that the Kurdish emirs tolerated and protected them.

Rome then added a third line. In 1672 Joseph, the church's archbishop at Diyarbakır, broke with the patriarch Elias. Labourt says he followed the advice of Capuchin missionaries. In 1681 Pope Innocent XI gave him the pallium and the title of patriarch. Wigram dates the new line to 1680.

Five men named Joseph held this see in turn. Badger says neither the old bishops nor the Ottoman government recognized the line at first. It did not reach beyond Diyarbakır.

In 1778 the line of the plain began to turn to Rome. Patriarch Elia died of plague at Alqosh on 29 April. His nephew Hormizd, a metropolitan, wrote the next part himself, in Badger's English: “So on the 30th of April I embraced all that the holy Church believes.” Another nephew, Yeshua-yau, was to be patriarch. Within a year he turned back, and the two became enemies. In 1782 Pope Pius VI let Hormizd act as patriarch, but not use the patriarch's seal.

The sources disagree on when the plain line truly joined Rome. Wigram puts it in 1778. Labourt puts it in 1830, after Rome had cut Hormizd off in 1818. Wigram says the Joseph line was then allowed to lapse, though its last holder lived until 1828.
entries.teaser: Diyarbakır, Mosul and the Hakkari mountains, 1650 to 1815. An ancient church with three patriarchs at once. In 1778 the patriarch's nephew turned to Rome.
voices: Yohannan Hormizd — nephew of the patriarch Elia, who tells in his own account how he turned to Rome on 30 April 1778
Joseph — archbishop of Diyarbakır, who broke with the patriarch Elias in 1672 and became the first of the Catholic patriarchs named Joseph
Elia — patriarch of the East at Alqosh and Mosul, who died of plague on 29 April 1778

entries.legacy: By 1815 the church stood divided. On the plain, Hormizd led a party in union with Rome, but Rome had not yet made him patriarch. The line of the mountains stayed outside Rome's obedience. Its later story is told in the entry on the Church of the East and the Chaldean Consolidation.

entries.name: The Maronite Church — Mountain, War and One Governor
entries.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1): the crisis of 1860 is a turning point for the whole region and is well recorded. The main sources are a Catholic study and a British officer who took the other side. Its window runs from 1815 to 1906. Not yet reviewed.
entries.sourcing:
The evidence is moderate, and it comes from outside the church.

Labourt wrote for a Catholic reference work. He tells the story from a Catholic view and calls other churches schismatic.

Churchill was a British colonel who had lived in the Lebanon. He took the side of the Druzes and wrote harshly of the Maronite patriarch.

No Maronite document from these years was opened.
entries.relationsSummary: This entry carries the Maronite Church from 1815 to 1906. It carries on the Maronite entry that ends in 1517; the years between are not yet told here. French missionaries and soldiers shaped these years.
entries.why: In 1860 the Druzes killed many Maronites, and France sent an army. A year later the mountain had one governor and no feudal lords.
entries.longDescription:
At the start of the nineteenth century the Maronites of Mount Lebanon lived under a feudal order. The great families chose the emir. In Europe they liked to be called princes. The patriarch sat at the cloister of St Mary at Kanobin.

That order broke in the 1840s. A fierce struggle with the Druzes began in 1845 and laid waste the whole Lebanon. Churchill, a British colonel, took the Druze side. In the heading of one chapter he wrote "Maronite Intrigues". Of the patriarch of the mid-1850s he wrote of "hatred to the feudal aristocracy, and a fanatic devotion to the religious tenets of his own sect". Labourt, a Catholic, tells it differently. He praises Patriarch Peter Paul Massaad, who served from 1855 to 1890, for a firmness that softened the shock of these conflicts.

In 1860 the Druzes killed a large number of Maronites at Damascus and in the Lebanon. Labourt says that France sent an army under General de Beaufort d'Hautpoult, and that it restored order. In 1861 the mountain got one governor for all the Lebanon. Labourt says that no feudal rights remained and that all were equal before the law.

The church changed inside too. In 1818 Patriarch Joseph Dolci and a synod ended the paired monasteries, one for men and one for women. French missionaries ran many schools in the Lebanon. Jesuits and Lazarists were among them. In 1899 the bishops elected Elias Hoyek patriarch.
entries.teaser: Mount Lebanon, 1815 to 1906. A mountain church that lost its feudal lords in a war, saw its people killed in 1860, and gained one governor in 1861.

entries.legacy: The Maronite Church is alive today. Its patriarch still has his see at Bkerke, and its bishops still meet in council.

entries.name: The Georgian Church — Between Persia, the Ottomans and Russia
entries.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2): the main account is a church history in English. The window runs from 1650 to 1811. That year the catholicate ended. Not yet reviewed.
entries.sourcing:
The evidence is moderate. The main source is a church history by Plato Ioselian. He wrote in Russian at Tiflis. Malan put it into English in 1866. Ioselian calls the missionaries' work "perverting".

Dowling's sketches of 1912 are an English churchman's. They print a Georgian appeal that tells the same years as a loss.

No Georgian-language text was opened.
entries.relationsSummary: This entry carries the Georgian Church from 1650 to 1811. The Georgian Golden Age comes long before it. The Russian Church Synodal Century tells what came next, when an exarch governed the church. Catholic missionaries and Russian protection shaped these years.
entries.why: The Georgian church stood between Persian, Ottoman and Russian power for a century and a half. In 1811 Russia ended its catholicate. An exarch took its place.
entries.longDescription:
For a century and a half the Georgian church lived between great powers. Dowling says Georgia "suffered severely from the attacks of Persians and Turks". Akhaltsikhe stayed Ottoman. In 1795 a Persian army took Tiflis and burned it. Ioselian says the churches were full of killers.

Catholic monks came too. Theatines came in 1625, and Capuchins followed. At first the kings used them as teachers. Ioselian says they "perverted" many.

Catholicos Antoni I left Georgia in 1755. The accounts differ on why. Ioselian says the king feared the catholicos meant to leave the Orthodox faith, so a synod gave him a choice: leave, or give up his office. Dowling says Antoni opposed the Latin innovations and was deposed for it. Both say he went to the Russian Synod. Ioselian says the Synod found his confession of faith fully Orthodox. He became archbishop of Vladimir and later came back to his old see.

The church still made its own books and hymns. Macrina, sister of King Teimuraz I, wrote hymns that were still sung when Ioselian wrote. Catholicos Antoni I translated many works. Under King Heraclius II the ties with Russia grew closer, and the catholicos took a seat in the Russian Holy Synod. He kept his title.

That ended in 1811. A Georgian appeal printed by Dowling says the last catholicos was called to St Petersburg in 1810 and never allowed home. In 1811 the office was abolished. An exarch took its place.
entries.teaser: Georgia, 1650 to 1811. A church caught between three powers. A catholicos fled in 1755. In 1811 the catholicate ended.
voices: Antoni I — catholicos who left Georgia in 1755, was cleared by the Russian Synod, and came back to his see
Macrina — sister of King Teimuraz I, whose hymns to the saints of Georgia were still sung when Ioselian wrote

set.longDescription:
When the Patriarch of Antioch died in 1724, the Christians of Damascus elected Cyril VI Tanas, who favored union with Rome. Constantinople refused to accept him and consecrated a rival, Sylvester, a Greek monk from Cyprus. The Antiochian patriarchate never reunited. What followed was the permanent division of one Arabic-speaking, Byzantine-rite community into two churches — one in communion with Rome, recognized by the pope in 1729, and one with Constantinople — sharing the same liturgy, the same language and frequently the same families. The Catholic side, based at Damascus, Aleppo and the monasteries of Mount Lebanon, was pressed hard by Ottoman authorities acting on Orthodox complaints, and was not granted a recognized civil standing of its own until well into the nineteenth century.

The split had a long run-up. In 1654 Patriarch Macarius of Antioch was in the Cossack lands. His journey took him to Kyiv and on to Moscow. His son Paul, an archdeacon of Aleppo, wrote the journey down.

Before 1724 some Orthodox bishops of Syria had tried to reach reunion with Rome. Fortescue, a Catholic writer, tells it. Euthymius, bishop of Tyre and Sidon, approached the Holy See. So did the patriarchs Athanasius IV and Cyril of Berrhoea. They hoped to receive the pallium. Rome found their professions of faith too weak. In 1722 a synod at Constantinople sent the Antiochene bishops a warning letter. It listed Latin heresies. No Orthodox account of these approaches to Rome was read.

Sylvester of Antioch — the Cypriot monk consecrated by Constantinople as the rival patriarch, who governed the Orthodox side of the split for nearly fifty years
Euthymios Saifi — bishop of Tyre and Sidon in the decades before the split, whose pro-Roman work and religious order prepared the ground for it
Macarius III of Antioch — patriarch whose journey to the Cossack lands and Moscow in the 1650s was written down by his son, Paul of Aleppo

For a century and a half after 1650 the Orthodox church of the Ottoman Empire was both a church and an arm of the state: the Ecumenical Patriarch in Constantinople answered to the Sultan for the obedience of all Orthodox subjects, collected their taxes and judged their marriages and inheritances. It was a position of real power and total insecurity — patriarchs were deposed and restored constantly. And it came increasingly to be held under the influence of the Phanariots, the wealthy Greek families of Constantinople's Phanar quarter who supplied the empire's interpreters and the princes of its Danubian provinces. In 1672 the Synod of Jerusalem, under Patriarch Dositheus, issued a confession answering the Calvinist ideas that had been circulating under an Orthodox name — the East's own equivalent of the West's confessional settlements. That power also worked against its neighbors: the Serbian patriarchate of Peć was abolished in 1766 and the archbishopric of Ohrid in 1767, both absorbed into Constantinople. It ended violently — when the Greek revolt broke out in 1821, Patriarch Gregory V was hanged in his vestments from the gate of his own patriarchate.

Not every Orthodox church of these years stood under Constantinople. Fortescue, a Catholic writer, lists two that stood apart. One is Karlovci, made of Orthodox Serbs in Hungary. He dates it to 1765. The other is Montenegro, with one independent diocese on the Black Mountain. He also dates it to 1765. His dates mark independence as he counts it.

A Bulgarian revival began in these years. In 1762 Paisii, a monk of Hilendar, wrote a history of the Bulgarians. Yordan Ivanov printed it in 1914. He says Paisii called to his readers: «Българино! знай своя родъ и езикъ» ("Bulgarian! know your own people and language", a rendering). Ivanov adds that Paisii named three causes of his people's spiritual ruin. They were no freedom, no national hierarchy and no national schools. Ivanov writes in the Bulgarian national tradition. He blames the Greek clergy. No Greek account of this dispute was read.

set.longDescription:
Under Ottoman rule, the Orthodox of the Balkans were governed as one religious community. That community answered to the Patriarch of Constantinople. The Greek revolt of 1821 broke this order apart. Weeks after the rising began, Patriarch Gregory V was hanged at the gate of his own home. As each new nation won its freedom, its church claimed the right to govern itself. Greece declared its church free in 1833, and Constantinople formally accepted it in 1850. Bulgaria won a decree from the sultan in 1870 that set up a national church, the exarchate. Serbia won its own church in 1879 and Romania in 1885. In 1872 a council at Constantinople condemned phyletism, which means building the church around a nation rather than a place. Even so, national churches kept on spreading. The century did not simply break one church apart. It made a family of churches. Each had its own synod, its own language of worship and its own claim on a people.

The call for a national church was older. Ivanov says the monk Paisii, writing in 1762, named the lack of a national hierarchy and national schools. He listed them among the causes of his people's spiritual ruin. The exarchate of 1870 was a national church.

Not every new Orthodox church grew out of the Ottoman patriarchate. Fortescue, a Catholic writer, dates a self-governing church of the Vlachs of Hungary to 1864. He calls it Hermannstadt. Today the town is Sibiu.

set.longDescription:
Patriarch Nikon, elected in 1652, set out to correct Russian service books against Greek models and to assert the priesthood's authority over the tsar's. And lost both fights: the corrections split the church permanently, and Nikon himself was deposed by the council of 1666-67 that condemned his opponents. Half a century later Peter the Great settled the second argument the other way. When the patriarch died in 1700 Peter simply left the office empty, and in 1721 he abolished it, replacing it with a Holy Synod of clergy, watched over by a lay official the tsar appointed. The church became, in effect, a department of the imperial government and stayed one for two hundred years. Catherine II completed the process in 1764 by confiscating the monastic estates. Yet the same church produced Tikhon of Zadonsk's gentle devotional writing, a serious seminary system, and in 1794 sent monks from Valaam across the Pacific to Alaska.

The church followed the Russian frontier east. The council of 1666 and 1667 raised Tobolsk, in Siberia, to a metropolitan see. It also proposed new bishoprics at Tomsk and on the Lena. They lay far from Tobolsk. In Peter the Great's reign, Mouravieff says, Theodore of Tobolsk converted 10,000 Ostiaks. The numbers are Mouravieff's, in an English version of 1842.

Governed under Metropolitan Filaret of Moscow and, later, the state-appointed ober-procurator Konstantin Pobedonostsev. Sent missions to the Altai peoples and to Japan (from 1861, under Nikolai), and reached the 1905 toleration edict that opened the way to the council that restored the patriarchate. The Optina elders' renewal movement grew within this church, and Alaska was one of its missions. It stood in tension with the separate Old Believer Belokrinitsa hierarchy, founded in 1846, and with the evangelical Stundist movement that broke from it.

After 1811 it also governed the Georgian church through an exarch.
set.longDescription:
For this whole century the Russian Orthodox Church had no patriarch. It was governed by a Holy Synod whose chief lay officer, the ober-procurator, answered to the tsar — an arrangement that produced both an immense institution and a cramped one. Metropolitan Filaret of Moscow gave Russia its standard catechism and pressed for decades for a Bible in modern Russian, finished in 1876 over long resistance. Missions went out to the Altai peoples, to Alaska and to Japan. Monasteries and their elders drew crowds, and a parish priest, John of Kronstadt, became the most sought-after confessor in the empire. But under Konstantin Pobedonostsev, ober-procurator for a quarter-century, the church was also the instrument of a policy of religious uniformity that pressed hard on Old Believers, Eastern Catholics and evangelicals alike. When toleration was finally decreed in 1905, the church immediately began preparing the council that would give it back its own head.

The church also governed Georgia. In 1811 the Georgian catholicate ended. Ioselian, a Georgian historian in Malan's English, says the head of the Georgian clergy then took the title "Member of the Synod, and Exarch of Georgia". The first to hold it was Archbishop Balaam. Ioselian calls him a Georgian of a princely family. A Georgian appeal calls him a Russian. In 1814 the emperor gave Balaam the exarchate of Imereti as well. In December 1818 one exarchy was set up for all Georgia. The same appeal says that Georgia's church lost its rights against canon law and that its property was seized. The Georgian church's later story is told in the entry on the restored Georgian church.

Missions went east too. Blackmore put Mouravieff's history into English in 1842. In its preface he wrote of the "marked success" of the missions in Siberia.

set.longDescription:
The Church of the East — the church that once sent bishops from Baghdad as far as China — entered this century reduced to the mountains and plains of the Ottoman-Persian borderland and divided between rival patriarchal lines, one in communion with Rome and one not. In 1830 Rome confirmed John Hormizd as patriarch of Babylon, consolidating the Chaldean Catholic Church as a single body. The line that stayed independent kept its seat in the mountain village of Qudshanis in Hakkari, its patriarchate passing from uncle to nephew, and its people came to be known as the Assyrian Church of the East. Both then found themselves courted by outsiders. American Congregationalist missionaries settled at Urmia in the 1830s and gave the region a printing press and schools in the spoken Syriac of the day. From 1886 the Archbishop of Canterbury sent a mission expressly instructed to strengthen the ancient church rather than convert its members.

A third outsider came in the 1890s. Wigram writes that in 1896 the part of the church living in Persia submitted to the mission the Russian Orthodox Church had sent to teach them. They hoped this would bring political protection. Wigram says it did, for as long as Russian power lasted. He adds that the Assyrians in Turkish lands began to think of following.
